title: IPA warns against turning super into govt funding source
full_text:
Australia’s superannuation pool should remain focused on delivering retirement outcomes rather than helping governments manage budget pressures, according to the Institute of Public Accountants (IPA), which has cautioned against any shift in the purpose of the nation’s retirement savings.
The warning comes as debate continues over whether Australia’s growing pool of super assets could play a larger role in supporting public spending priorities.
While the IPA acknowledged super funds can invest in infrastructure, it argued those investments must be assessed on the same commercial basis as any other asset and remain focused on members’ returns.
“If the government is intent on dipping into Australia’s superannuation pool to fund infrastructure projects, it would have to be evaluated like any other investment, be in superannuation fund members’ best interests and maximise returns to boost retirement savings.”
The IPA added Australia’s super system, which holds approximately $4.5 trillion in retirement savings across more than 18 million accounts, was established to reduce reliance on the Age Pension and provide financial security in retirement.
It said treating those savings as a source of government funding risked undermining confidence in the system.
“Superannuation is not a ‘national asset’. It is not an ATM for governments facing fiscal challenges. Superannuation is the hard-earned retirement savings of millions of Australians who have sacrificed current income to provide for their future.”
IPA general manager advocacy and emerging policy, Michael Davison, said Australians had spent decades building their retirement savings and should not be expected to absorb the cost of rising government expenditure.
He argued governments should instead address long-term fiscal challenges through budget management rather than looking to super.
“Australians had spent decades building their retirement savings and should not be expected to bear the cost of government spending pressures.”
“Governments must address structural spending challenges through sound fiscal management rather than viewing superannuation as a convenient source of funding.”
The IPA also warned against setting a precedent that could change expectations about the role of super.
Australians contribute throughout their working lives with the expectation their retirement savings will be preserved, the organisation said, adding that confidence in the system could be eroded if governments sought to redirect those assets for public spending.
“Australians contribute to superannuation throughout their working lives on the expectation that these savings will be preserved and maximised for their retirement. Any attempt to treat superannuation as a honey pot for government expenditure risks undermining confidence in the entire system.”
Australians drew $143.5 billion in retirement benefits in the 12 months to March 2026, reflecting the growing importance of superannuation in funding retirement. Against that backdrop, Davison warned that using super to fill budget gaps could have consequences beyond the current fiscal environment.
“Today it may be justified by government as a solution to a funding gap. Tomorrow it could become a precedent for future governments looking for easy answers to difficult budget problems. That is a dangerous path which threatens the retirement security of current and future generations.
“Super exists to help Australians achieve dignity and independence in retirement. Governments should be strengthening trust in the system, not creating uncertainty around it.”
Davison said using superannuation to solve immediate funding pressures could establish an undesirable precedent.
“Today it may be justified by [the] government as a solution to a funding gap. Tomorrow it could become a precedent for future governments looking for easy answers to difficult budget problems. That is a dangerous path which threatens the retirement security of current and future generations.”
He said governments should instead reinforce confidence in the retirement system, adding: “Super exists to help Australians achieve dignity and independence in retirement. Governments should be strengthening trust in the system, not creating uncertainty around it.”
